newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's two biggest parties nearly level in polls.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's two biggest parties nearly level in polls.

text.p: Public support for Sweden's ruling Social Democrats and the opposition conservative party, the Moderates, is almost level for the first time since the 1994 election, according to a survey published on Sunday.

The poll, conducted in December by the Swedish Institute for Public Opinion and Research, Sifo, found there is only half a percentage point difference between the country's two biggest parties with the next election due in autumn 1998.
Support for the Social Democrats, who hold about 46 percent of the 349 seats in parliament, fell by 3.1 percentage points in December to 29.6 procent.
Sifo said support for the Social Democrats has not been so low since April 1991.
At the general election in 1994 the Social Democrats led by Ingvar Carlsson won 45.3 percent of the vote.
But since Goran Persson took over the party leadership in March this year, support has fallen continuously.

It has slipped even further since an unsuccessful vote of no confidence was levelled at Persson in November over allegedly complimentary comments he made about China's political stability during a trip to Beijing.
The Moderates, however, have become more popular, despite party leader Carl Bildt's absence due to his work in Bosnia.
The survey of 2,800 people found 29.1 percent would vote for the Moderates if a new election was held now which was a rise of 2.7 percentage points since November.
The Moderates hold about 26.4 percent of seats in the current parliament.
Among the five other parties in parliament, the Left Party has seen support increase, getting 14.7 percent of the vote in the December survey which was a lift of 1.3 percentage points from November.
The Centre Party, which has an informal alliance with the Social Democrats, saw support rise 0.4 percentage points to seven percent.
The Green Party slipped 0.3 percentage points to 7.8 percent while the Liberals' support dipped 0.3 percentage points to 5.8 percent.
Support for the Christian Democrats was unchanged at 4.6 percent.
The rest of the people surveyed were undecided or would not vote for any of the seven parties currently in parliament.
